kurz: US funds pay out their income every year, and you owe tax on it even if it is reinvested; what matters is the type of distribution, your tax bracket and the account that holds the fund.

bloecke.md:
In Europe, many index funds come in two share classes, one that distributes its income and one that accumulates it, that is, reinvests it inside the fund. In the US, this choice practically does not exist. ETFs and mutual funds registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 are taxed as regulated investment companies (RICs). They avoid tax at fund level only if they distribute at least 90% of their net investment income, and an excise tax pushes them to pay out practically all income and realized gains every year (26 U.S.C. §§ 852 and 4982). A US index fund therefore always distributes. What you choose instead is what happens to the money afterwards, cash in your account or automatic reinvestment, and in which account the fund sits.

On the ex-dividend date, the fund's price falls by the amount of the distribution. An investor with 100 shares at $120 who receives $1.50 per share then has $150 in cash and 100 shares at $118.50, so their wealth is unchanged. If the dividend is reinvested automatically, the $150 buys about 1.27 new shares. Differences in portfolio value after twenty years therefore arise only from taxes and from costs and delays in reinvestment.

A distribution does not increase wealth. It moves money from the fund to your account and, in a taxable account, turns part of the fund's return into taxable income for that year, whether or not you reinvest it.

## How distributions are taxed

Your broker reports the distributions on Form 1099-DIV at the start of the following year. Three kinds matter. **Qualified dividends** (box 1b) are taxed at the same federal rates as long-term capital gains, that is 0%, 15% or 20% (26 U.S.C. § 1(h)(11)). For that, you must have held the fund shares for more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date, and the fund itself must have received qualifying dividends, mainly from US companies and many foreign companies. **Ordinary dividends** that are not qualified, such as interest passed through by bond funds, most REIT dividends and distributed short-term gains, are taxed like wages at your [[Marginal tax rate|marginal tax rate]]. **Capital gain distributions** (box 2a) are always taxed as long-term gains, no matter how long you have owned the fund.

Above a modified adjusted gross income of $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (married filing jointly), the net investment income tax (NIIT) of 3.8% applies on top (26 U.S.C. § 1411). These thresholds are not indexed to inflation. Most states tax dividends as ordinary income as well; a few have no income tax at all.

bloecke.erklaerung: The tax is due for the year in which the distribution is paid, even if it is reinvested the same day. In an IRA, a 401(k) or another tax-advantaged account, distributions are not taxed when they are paid. A traditional account taxes withdrawals later as ordinary income, a Roth account not at all if the withdrawal is qualified.

bloecke.md:
## Distributions in good and bad years

The tax on a distribution does not depend on how the fund performed. A dividend is paid and taxed in a year in which the fund lost 15% just as in a year in which it gained 20%. With broad stock index ETFs, the distribution consists almost entirely of dividends. Mutual funds, and especially actively managed ones, can also pay out realized capital gains, sometimes in a year in which their price fell. ETFs rarely have to do this. When shares are redeemed, they can hand over securities with large unrealized gains to market makers in kind, and under 26 U.S.C. § 852(b)(6) this does not trigger a gain at fund level.

bloecke.md: Illustrative calculation with fully qualified dividends of 1.5%, a 15% rate, no NIIT and no state tax. The tax on a distribution is not an additional burden over the whole holding period. A reinvested dividend buys new shares whose cost basis equals the amount reinvested, so less gain is taxed when you sell later. The distribution merely moves part of the tax forward in time. Money that goes to the IRS today no longer compounds in your account, and that is the entire cost, often called tax drag.

bloecke.titel: $50,000 over 30 years at 7%: dividends taxed every year or not (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: Total return of 7% a year, of which 1.5% are dividends taxed at 15% every year in the taxable account. After 30 years, the taxable account is worth around $357,000 instead of around $381,000, before tax on unrealized gains. Part of the gap is recovered on a sale, because the reinvested dividends have raised the cost basis.

serien.name: No tax on dividends along the way (e.g. Roth IRA)

bloecke.md: Reinvested distributions are taxable income even though no money reaches your bank account. With a large taxable portfolio, the federal tax on several thousand dollars of distributions is due by April 15 or through estimated tax payments during the year. Plan the cash for it, or have the distributions paid out instead of reinvested and use part of them to pay the tax.

## The 0% bracket

The US has no separate allowance for investment income. The closest counterpart is the 0% bracket for qualified dividends and long-term capital gains. These amounts are stacked on top of your other taxable income, and whatever part of them still fits under the 0% threshold is free of federal income tax. A single filer whose only deduction is the standard deduction ($16,100 in 2026) can therefore have total income of up to $65,550 and still pay 0% on qualified dividends and long-term gains, because taxable income then stays at $49,450. For married couples filing jointly, the corresponding figures are a standard deduction of $32,200 and total income of up to $131,100.

The table also explains why, in the US, the choice of account matters more than the form of distribution. Retirees and people in years with low income can often realize dividends and gains at 0%. In the 15% bracket and above, it pays to hold tax-inefficient funds in an IRA or 401(k) and broad stock ETFs in the taxable account. This is called asset location, and it saves more than any other decision around distributions.

## The effort of reinvestment

At US brokers, automatic dividend reinvestment, often called DRIP, is usually a single setting and buys fractional shares without a commission. Without it, the cash sits in the settlement fund or the cash sweep until you place an order. If you collect it and invest it once a quarter, little is lost. In the 15% bracket, a distribution of $900 leaves $765 for reinvestment after federal tax.

bloecke.md:
## Distribution and partial sale in the withdrawal phase

A common piece of advice for retirement is to live off dividends. The money then flows in without any action on your part, nobody has to sell shares in a crash, and the number of shares in the portfolio is preserved. This is psychologically convincing and organizationally simple. In a taxable account, however, it is the more expensive route, because a dividend is 100% income, while in a sale only the gain portion is taxed. US rules also let you choose which shares you sell. With the specific identification method, you can sell the lots with the highest cost basis first (Treas. Reg. § 1.1012-1(c)).

A taxable portfolio is worth $400,000 and the cost basis is $200,000, so the gain portion is 50%. The investor needs $10,000 and is in the 15% bracket for long-term gains.

- If the $10,000 comes from qualified dividends, the full amount is income, and the federal tax is $1,500.
- With a sale of shares held for more than a year, $10,000 of proceeds contains $5,000 of gain at the average basis, and the tax is $750. Selling the lots with the highest basis first lowers it further.

Here the sale costs half as much. The longer the portfolio runs, the higher the gain portion and the smaller the gap. With a gain portion of 70%, the sale costs $1,050, while the dividend route still costs $1,500. Investors in the 0% bracket pay nothing either way, and investors who spend every dividend anyway lose nothing extra. If, on the other hand, only part of the dividends is needed and the rest is reinvested, money has been taxed that could have stayed in the portfolio.

bloecke.titel: Switching funds and buying a distribution
bloecke.md:
Switching from a mutual fund to an ETF on the same index in a taxable account is a sale followed by a new purchase. The tax on the entire accumulated gain becomes due at once, and the deferral built up over years is used up. It is usually cheaper to direct new contributions and distributions to the new fund and to leave the existing holding untouched.

A second trap concerns mutual funds that announce a capital gain distribution in December. If you buy shortly before the record date, part of your own money comes back to you as a taxable distribution. In an IRA or 401(k), neither point matters, because trades and distributions inside the account are not taxed.

1. Decide where each fund belongs before the first purchase. Bond funds, REIT funds and actively managed funds with high distributions fit better into an IRA or 401(k); broad stock index ETFs are the most tax-efficient holding for a taxable account.
2. Choose between automatic reinvestment and cash payouts. Having distributions paid out in cash and investing them in whatever part of the portfolio is underweight is a simple way to rebalance.
3. Set your cost basis method at the broker before you sell anything. Many brokers default to first in, first out; specific identification must be chosen at the latest when the sale is made.
4. Check Form 1099-DIV in February. It shows how much of the distribution was qualified, ordinary or a capital gain distribution, and how much foreign tax the fund paid.

Bond funds, money market funds and REIT funds distribute mostly ordinary income, which is taxed at your marginal tax rate. Interest from US Treasury securities is exempt from state income tax, and municipal bond funds pay dividends that are generally exempt from federal income tax. REIT dividends that are not qualified can be eligible for a 20% deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 199A, which the 2025 tax law made permanent.

International stock funds pay foreign withholding tax on the dividends they receive. If more than half of the fund's assets are foreign stocks, the fund can pass this tax through to you (26 U.S.C. § 853), and you can claim a foreign tax credit, without Form 1116 up to $300 ($600 if married filing jointly). In an IRA or 401(k), this credit is lost.

Accumulating funds domiciled outside the US, for example European UCITS ETFs with ISINs beginning with IE or LU, are passive foreign investment companies (PFICs) for US persons (26 U.S.C. § 1297). Without an election, gains on a sale and large distributions are allocated over the holding period and taxed largely at the highest ordinary rate of each year, plus an interest charge, and Form 8621 has to be filed every year. A qualified electing fund (QEF) election would avoid this, but it requires an annual information statement that most European providers do not issue. US persons living in Europe run into this rule most often.

mitnehmen: A distribution changes nothing about your wealth; in a taxable account it moves part of the tax forward to the year of payment, even if the money is reinvested.
Regular US funds always distribute, because regulated investment companies must pay out practically all income; accumulating foreign funds are PFICs and a costly mistake for US persons.
Qualified dividends and capital gain distributions are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, plus 3.8% NIIT above $200,000 or $250,000 of income; ordinary dividends at the marginal tax rate.
The 0% bracket (taxable income up to $49,450 single or $98,900 joint in 2026) and the choice of account (asset location) matter more than the form of distribution.
In the withdrawal phase, selling shares is more tax-efficient than living off dividends, because only the gain portion is taxed and you can choose the lots with the highest cost basis.

begriffe.text: Reinvestment of income within the fund instead of a payout. Common for European UCITS funds; regular US funds distribute practically all income because of the rules for regulated investment companies.

Dividend taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates of 0%, 15% or 20%. It requires a holding period of more than 60 days within the 121-day window around the ex-dividend date and a dividend from a US company or a qualifying foreign company. Reported in box 1b of Form 1099-DIV.
Payout of gains a fund realized by selling securities. It is taxed as a long-term capital gain regardless of how long you have held the fund. Rare for index ETFs, more common for mutual funds.

Foreign company with mainly passive income or assets under 26 U.S.C. § 1297. Almost all funds domiciled outside the US, including UCITS ETFs, qualify. For US persons, a PFIC leads to punitive taxation unless a QEF or mark-to-market election is made, and to annual reporting on Form 8621.
The amount paid for an investment, including commissions and reinvested distributions. Only the difference between the sale proceeds and the cost basis is a taxable gain.
